---
title: "Path C · The Crossover"
subtitle: "Read a modeling report without bluffing"
---

**For:** bench pharmacologists, clinicians, DMPK and translational scientists,
statisticians, data scientists, project leaders — anyone who has to act on
modeling results without producing them.

**Promise:** you can read a population PK report, know what each plot does and
does not establish, and ask the questions that find the problems.

**Ends at:** competence as a reader and a reviewer. That is a complete,
legitimate destination. Branch into Path A or B afterwards if you want to build
models yourself.

## Start here if the biology is not yours

If you have arrived from statistics, mathematics, engineering or software, the
vocabulary is the barrier, not the mathematics. Work
[**Strand P · Pharmacology from the beginning**](../pharmacology.qmd) first —
it assumes nothing, and `P-01` to `P-05` alone will make everything below
readable. For many people on this path, `P` plus `S0-06` is the entire
destination.

If pharmacology is already yours and it is the quantitative framing you want,
skip straight to the short route.

## The short route — about four hours

| | Lesson | Read for |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | [S0-00 · What quantitative pharmacology is](../lessons/s0-00-what-is-qp/index.qmd) | Sections 1–4: the vocabulary, the four questions, the modeling families, and where models enter a programme. Skip the career sections unless they interest you. |
| 2 | [S0-06 · Reading a model report](../lessons/s0-06-reading-a-model-report/index.qmd) | All of it. This is the keystone lesson. |
| 3 | [S0-02 · Units, scaling and allometry](../lessons/s0-02-units-scaling-and-allometry/index.qmd) | Sections 3–7: molar versus mass, free versus total, and the honest answer to "should we dose per kilogram?" |

Take the twelve questions from S0-06 into your next model review meeting. They
work without any modeling ability at all, and question 9 — *is the simulated
scenario inside the range of the observed data?* — finds more real problems than
the rest combined.

## If you never model, these are still worth bookmarking

This path is allowed to end here, and for many readers it should. Four free
resources remain useful even if you never fit a model (all on
[Resources](../resources.qmd)):

- [Drugs@FDA](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cder/daf/) — the clinical
  pharmacology review behind an approval. If a modeller shows you a report and
  you want to see what a good one looks like, read a review for a drug you
  already know.
- [IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY](https://www.guidetopharmacology.org/) — a
  curated, referenced affinity value when someone quotes you an IC~50~ with no
  assay conditions attached. `P-04` explains why that matters.
- [FDA Table of Substrates, Inhibitors and Inducers](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-interactions-labeling/drug-development-and-drug-interactions-table-substrates-inhibitors-and-inducers)
  — the regulatorily accepted probe drugs, in one table.
- [ICH M15](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/m15-general-principles-model-informed-drug-development)
  (final, June 2026) — the shortest statement of what regulators now expect a
  model to justify. If you sit in meetings where models are discussed, this is
  the document that tells you what question to ask.

## The three things worth remembering

1. **A compartment is not an organ.** It is a kinetically homogeneous space
   chosen to reproduce the data, not a claim about anatomy.
2. **Clearance sets the maintenance dose; volume sets the loading dose.**
   Half-life is derived from both and is a poor thing to reason with.
3. **Statistical significance of a covariate is not a dose recommendation.**
   The question is always magnitude relative to the therapeutic window.
